Family memorial sheet · not an official publication Quang Tri Province · RVN · Sheet ref 6342-III

Lawrence Himmer

CAPTAIN · USMC · CO, COMPANY C, 1ST BN, 9TH MARINES · 23 JUL 1938 — 16 APR 1968 · THE WALL, PANEL 50E · LINE 14

Husband of Sharon. Father of five — the youngest born six weeks after he fell. Killed leading his company up a nameless hill southwest of Khe Sanh, going to the relief of other Marines.

“Was with Charlie Company the day the Skipper died. Will never forget.” — Jim Thompson, C/1/9, remembrance left at the Wall of Faces, 2020 [4]

Sheet I · The Man

Larry

Lawrence “Larry” Himmer was 29, from Chula Vista, California, on his third tour in Vietnam.[4] Family remembrances describe a gifted artist and an easy people-person — loving, considerate, quick with an encouraging word — an active Latter-day Saint who held the office of Elder, devoted to his parents and siblings.[4] He wrote home to his four children — Richard, Dale, Teresa, and LaShel — telling them to mind their mother, Sharon, who was expecting. Jennifer Lana Himmer was born May 31, 1968, six weeks after her father was killed.[4]

His ribbon set includes the Good Conduct Medal — an award only enlisted Marines can earn — which points to a start in the ranks and a commission earned later: what the Corps calls a Mustang.[5] It fits the man the records show: a 29-year-old captain, three tours deep, commanding a rifle company. Before his last tour, the family recalls, he left with his affairs in order.[4]

Photographs · from the Wall of Faces

Eleven photographs posted by family at the VVMF Wall of Faces. Tap any photo to open the original. If frames show blank here, this preview is blocking outside images — open the file in your browser and they’ll appear.

Sheet II · The Battalion

The Walking Dead

1st Battalion, 9th Marines carried the highest killed-in-action rate of any Marine battalion in history: of 2,892 Marines and corpsmen who served in it across 47 months in Vietnam, 747 were killed — 25.89 percent.[15] Through the first months of 1968 the battalion helped hold Khe Sanh Combat Base through the 77-day siege, dug in at the Rock Quarry west of the base under fire that ran to hundreds of incoming rounds a day.[1]

The siege was lifted by Operation Pegasus in early April. In its closing days 1/9 went back on the offensive, taking Hill 552 on 7 April and Hill 689 on 8 April against accurate mortar fire.[1] On 15 April 1968 at 8:00 AM, Operation Scotland II opened. Surviving the siege had been the first fight; holding Khe Sanh was the second — and holding it meant leaving the wire to take back the hills the NVA had watched, mortared, and rocketed the base from for 77 days.[7] 1/9, under LtCol John “Blackie” Cahill (in command since 1 April), set its battalion perimeter and operations center on Hill 689.[1][3]

77 daysSiege of Khe Sanh
25.89%1/9 killed in action, 1965–69
3rdLarry’s Vietnam tour

Reading the unit names

1/9 means the 1st Battalion of the 9th Marine Regiment — “the 9th Marines.” A battalion ran to roughly a thousand men on paper and was led by a lieutenant colonel — Cahill. It held four rifle companies, Alpha, Bravo, Charlie, and Delta, each about 215 men on paper under a captain. So C/1/9 reads “Company C, 1st Battalion, 9th Marines” — Larry’s command. Above the battalion sat the regiment, and above that the 3rd Marine Division. Alpha, Charlie, and Delta fought the battle of 16 April; Bravo’s station that day isn’t recorded in the public accounts.

Sheet III · The Ground

Two miles west of Khe Sanh

Everything on this sheet sits within four miles. Khe Sanh Combat Base on its plateau; the Rock Quarry at its western edge, 1/9’s home through the siege; Hill 552 and Hill 689 on the ridge running west — both taken by 1/9 in early April; and, about a mile southwest of Hill 689, the unnamed elephant-grass ridge the official history calls only “a small adjoining hill.” The Marines who fought there knew it by its map elevation, Hill 600 — and afterward as Dead Man’s Hill.[1][3]

Hill 689 was where 1/9 lived — the perimeter, the CP, the ops center. The battle of 16 April was fought on the other hill, a mile to its southwest.[1][3]

Sheet IV · The Battle

16 April 1968

Why send a patrol at all? Because the ridge a mile southwest looked straight down on 1/9’s week-old perimeter, and dominant ground works both ways: whoever holds it sees everything below, registers mortars on everything below, stages from cover against everything below. Scotland II existed precisely to sweep the NVA off such hills, and no battalion could leave that one unexamined. So Alpha’s sweep went out to answer one question — had the NVA come back into these hills?[1][7]

That morning, Army air-cavalry scouts finishing Operation Pegasus spotted what the Marines most needed to know: all elements of the NVA 66th Regiment, 304th Division, had moved back into the hills near Route 9 and Lang Vei. The report never reached Marine commanders.[3] So when Company A stepped off its patrol at 7:00 AM, battalion believed the ridge a mile southwest held perhaps a squad. It held a fortified complex of a regiment that had been digging for weeks. Alpha was marched out to discover, on foot and by fire, what the Army’s own scouts had already seen from the air.

The intelligence gap · morning, 16 April
The question

Alpha’s patrol existed to learn whether the NVA had reoccupied the hills over Khe Sanh. The answer was already in American hands before the first Marine stepped off.

What was seen

Army air-cavalry scouts of the 1st Cavalry Division, closing out Operation Pegasus, observed the NVA repopulating the hills around Khe Sanh — all elements of the 66th Regiment, 304th Division, a regiment blooded in the siege, back in the sector near Route 9 and Lang Vei.[3]

Where it went

Nowhere. The sighting was radioed within Army channels, but in the seam of the Army–Marine handoff between Pegasus and Scotland II it was never passed to the Marine commanders running the patrols.[3]

What 1/9 believed

That the ridge held an NVA squad — perhaps a dozen men. Capt Banks reported exactly that from the fight, and twice waved off help on that basis.[2]

What was waiting

Elements of that regiment in a reverse-slope, horseshoe-shaped bunker complex — concealed in the elephant grass, mutually supporting, sited to stay invisible until a unit was inside the kill zone. Marines on the hill judged it a heavily reinforced company at the least, possibly a battalion.[2][3]

The consequence

The cavalry saw the force; nobody could see the bunkers. The one warning that existed died between two services, so Alpha walked into the complex blind — and Charlie and Delta were committed against it still believing the enemy was small.

Use the phase buttons to replay the day on the map.

The approach, in numbers

A note on the famous “1,800 feet”: the veteran account describes Charlie at the 1,800-foot mark of a nearly 2,000-foot hill — an elevation reading, not a vertical climb. It can’t be a gain figure, because the company started on Hill 689, which stands higher (2,261 ft) than the objective (≈1,969 ft). The real profile was a descent off 689, a saddle crossing, and a final pitch of a few hundred feet up through elephant grass — steep, hot, under fire, in flak gear.[3]

Daily journal · reconstructed · 16–17 April 1968
Morning

Army air cavalry sights elements of the NVA 66th Regiment, 304th Division, back in the hills near Route 9 and Lang Vei. The report is never passed to Marine commanders.[3]

7:00 AM

Capt Henry D. Banks leads two reinforced platoons of Company A southwest off the Hill 689 perimeter — a clearing sweep of the high ground overlooking the battalion’s new position.[2]

10:00 AM

Company A halts; two squads push onto a ridge in four-to-six-foot elephant grass and take small-arms and mortar fire from concealed bunkers. The first Marines fall.[2]

~10:30 AM

1stLt Michael P. Hayden’s 2d Platoon assaults; Hayden and then his platoon sergeant are killed in rapid succession. Alpha is pinned on the north end of the ridge — 10 dead, 20 wounded. Banks twice declines offered help, believing he faces a squad.[2]

~Noon

Banks reverses and asks for relief.[2]

1:20 PM

LtCol Cahill commits Companies C and D. (His message doesn’t reach the regimental commander, Col Meyers, until 3:43 PM — the radio-relay fog of that day.)[2]

~2:00 PM

Two platoons of Company C move out first — Capt Himmer leading, Cahill accompanying — down off 689, across the saddle, and up the objective’s grassy slope: about a mile southwest in a straight line, nearer a mile and a half on foot with the swing to the south (est.).[2][3]

~2:30 PM

Charlie pauses at the hill’s 1,800-foot line, roughly fifty yards below the crest, waiting for orders. Finding Alpha immobile on the north end, Cahill “ordered Himmer to attack from the south” — the veteran account has Charlie moving onto the eastern-southeastern ridge — while Delta presses from the northwest.[2][3]

Afternoon

The relief attack bogs down in crossfire from bunkers, spider holes, and B-52 craters. Alpha’s dead and wounded are withdrawn. Somewhere on this southern approach, Captain Lawrence Himmer is killed leading his company. One of his Marines, PFC David Dee Brown Jr — four days in country — falls on the southern side of the hill.[3][13]

5:45 PM

Cahill orders every man off the hill with the wounded. The dead stay behind — “We will get them later.”[3]

Night–4 AM

Entangled with the NVA in the dark, the companies work free and fall back northeast to Hill 689, completing the withdrawal in the early morning of 17 April.[1][7]

Sheet V · The Cost

Thirty-eight Marines, three corpsmen

Killed in action, 16–17 April38 USMC + 3 USN
Missing3
Wounded32
Recovery sweep by 2/3 Marines, four days later — the dead brought home+6 KIA · 86 WIA
July 1968: 1/1 Marines recover earlier dead at Hill 689 during the base evacuation+11 KIA

Official-history figures.[1][7] A veterans’ memorial page gives differing tallies for 16–19 April (9 KIA / 46 WIA / 36 MIA), likely reflecting confused initial field reporting; the official figures are treated as authoritative.[8]

Roughly one man in five who went up those slopes became a casualty in a single afternoon — among the worst days any Marine battalion endured in 1968. The battalion commander, LtCol John “Blackie” Cahill, was relieved of duty afterward; the roster shows his command passing to LtCol James W. Quinn on 13 May.[1][7] The official history states no reason. The record cuts both ways: he declined offered reinforcements and fed companies into a fortified position — yet the intelligence that would have changed everything was withheld above his level, and his caution about recovering the dead was echoed days later by regiment and division, who themselves suspended rescue attempts as too costly.[2][3] Cahill — Chosin Reservoir veteran, Silver Star, four Purple Hearts — retired a colonel and died in 2005.[9]

Sheet VI · Coming Home

Fort Rosecrans, Point Loma

Captain Himmer was brought home to San Diego and buried at Fort Rosecrans National Cemetery, Plot Q 1222, above the water at Point Loma — a few miles from Chula Vista.[14] His decorations include the Purple Heart, Combat Action Ribbon, Good Conduct Medal, National Defense Service Medal, Vietnam Service Medal, and Vietnam Campaign Medal.[5] His name is cut into Panel 50E, Line 14 of the Vietnam Veterans Memorial, among the men of the 16th of April.[4]

Six weeks after he fell, Jennifer was born. Fifty-two years after that, a Marine who had been on the hill found his page on the Wall of Faces and left eleven words about the Skipper. His company remembered him. His family still does.

Sources

  2. The same volume, p. 313 read verbatim (incl. footnoted post-war comments by Col Bruce F. Meyers): eHistory, Ohio State — p. 313 (pp. 314–316 adjacent).
  3. John McGuire, “Rescuing the Walking Dead,” Vietnam magazine (Feb 2020), via HistoryNet — first-person account of Cpl Tommy “Hatch” Hatcher, 1st Plt, C/1/9; the “Hill 600” designation, the intelligence failure, and Cahill’s withdrawal order.
  4. Vietnam Veterans Memorial Fund, Wall of Faces — Lawrence Himmer, profile 23298 (service data, photos, family and veteran remembrances).
  5. The Virtual Wall — Capt Lawrence Himmer (unit, decorations; generated from the Coffelt Database).
  6. HonorStates.org — Lawrence Himmer, record 278291.
  7. Wikipedia, “Operation Scotland II” (summarizing Shulimson pp. 313–316; operation dates and casualty totals).
  8. Ray Smith, “Hill 689” (grid XD 803-409; unofficial casualty tallies) and Ray’s Map Room.
  9. San Diego Union-Tribune obituary, Col John J. H. “Blackie” Cahill (d. 14 July 2005), via Legacy.com.
  10. Military Wiki, “Operation Scotland II” (Hill 689 coordinates 16°38′35″N 106°41′20″E).
  11. U.S. Army Map Service 1:50,000 Sheet 6342-III “Huong Hoa” — UT Perry-Castañeda Vietnam topographic collection (the sheet the Marines used; grid keyed on both maps above).
  12. 1st Bn 9th Marines Command Chronology, April 1968 — Texas Tech Vietnam Center & Sam Johnson Vietnam Archive, document 1201056016 (primary daily journal; grids and command roster).
  13. University of Denver, “More Than A Headstone” — profile of PFC David Dee Brown Jr., C/1/9 (killed 16 Apr 1968, southern side of the hill).
  14. Fort Rosecrans National Cemetery interment record, Plot Q 1222; Find A Grave memorial 3406664.
  15. Military.com, feature on 1/9 “The Walking Dead” (24 Oct 2025) and battalion unit history (747 of 2,892 killed — 25.89%).

Reliability notes

Sourced facts above trace to the official history, the memorial databases, or period records. Derived: the battle hill’s position (≈ XD 792 398) is plotted one mile southwest of Hill 689 per the veteran account — not read from a period grid; the real 6342-III sheet would refine it. Approximate: Hill 552, the Rock Quarry, Khe Sanh village, Delta’s start point, and the medevac LZ are placed from narrative relationships. Unit routes are schematic — faithful to the documented sequence and directions, not to a surveyed trace. The name “Hill 600” is the Marines’ field designation; the official history leaves the ridge unnumbered. Casualty figures vary between sources as flagged in Sheet V. Larry’s role as C Company’s commanding officer rests on the official history’s account of Cahill’s order to him, his rank, and a Charlie Company veteran’s “Skipper” remembrance; the April 1968 command chronology’s staff roster would confirm it beyond doubt. Elevations for Hills 689 and 600 come from their map designations (meters converted to feet); the terrain profile’s connecting slopes and saddle are schematic at ≈2× vertical exaggeration, and the on-foot route length is an estimate built from the documented southern hook. The account’s “1,800 feet” is read here as an elevation line rather than a climb, since Charlie started on ground ≈290 ft higher than the objective.

For the family record

The two documents that will deepen this sheet: Larry’s Official Military Personnel File (request as next-of-kin from the National Personnel Records Center, St. Louis, via Standard Form 180 — Marine records survived the 1973 fire) and the 1/9 Command Chronology for April 1968 (Texas Tech document 1201056016), which holds the daily journal, exact grids, and the officer roster for the day he died.

Family memorial sheet · not an official publication Quang Tri Province · RVN · Sheet ref 6342-III

Lawrence Himmer

CAPTAIN · USMC · CO, COMPANY C, 1ST BN, 9TH MARINES · 23 JUL 1938 — 16 APR 1968 · THE WALL, PANEL 50E · LINE 14

Husband of Sharon. Father of five — the youngest born six weeks after he fell. Killed leading his company up a nameless hill southwest of Khe Sanh, going to the relief of other Marines.

“Was with Charlie Company the day the Skipper died. Will never forget.” — Jim Thompson, C/1/9, remembrance left at the Wall of Faces, 2020 [4]

Sheet I · The Man

Larry

Lawrence “Larry” Himmer was 29, from Chula Vista, California, on his third tour in Vietnam.[4] Family remembrances describe a gifted artist and an easy people-person — loving, considerate, quick with an encouraging word — an active Latter-day Saint who held the office of Elder, devoted to his parents and siblings.[4] He wrote home to his four children — Richard, Dale, Teresa, and LaShel — telling them to mind their mother, Sharon, who was expecting. Jennifer Lana Himmer was born May 31, 1968, six weeks after her father was killed.[4]

His ribbon set includes the Good Conduct Medal — an award only enlisted Marines can earn — which points to a start in the ranks and a commission earned later: what the Corps calls a Mustang.[5] It fits the man the records show: a 29-year-old captain, three tours deep, commanding a rifle company. Before his last tour, the family recalls, he left with his affairs in order.[4]

Sheet II · The Battalion

The Walking Dead

1st Battalion, 9th Marines carried the highest killed-in-action rate of any Marine battalion in history: of 2,892 Marines and corpsmen who served in it across 47 months in Vietnam, 747 were killed — 25.89 percent.[15] Through the first months of 1968 the battalion helped hold Khe Sanh Combat Base through the 77-day siege, dug in at the Rock Quarry west of the base under fire that ran to hundreds of incoming rounds a day.[1]

The siege was lifted by Operation Pegasus in early April. In its closing days 1/9 went back on the offensive, taking Hill 552 on 7 April and Hill 689 on 8 April against accurate mortar fire.[1] On 15 April 1968 at 0800, Operation Scotland II opened — the Marines pushing out to clear the hills the NVA had held around the base.[7] 1/9, under LtCol John “Blackie” Cahill (in command since 1 April), set its battalion perimeter and operations center on Hill 689.[1][3]

77 daysSiege of Khe Sanh
25.89%1/9 killed in action, 1965–69
3rdLarry’s Vietnam tour

Sheet III · The Ground

Two miles west of Khe Sanh

Everything on this sheet sits within four miles. Khe Sanh Combat Base on its plateau; the Rock Quarry at its western edge, 1/9’s home through the siege; Hill 552 and Hill 689 on the ridge running west — both taken by 1/9 in early April; and, about a mile southwest of Hill 689, the unnamed elephant-grass ridge the official history calls only “a small adjoining hill.” The Marines who fought there knew it by its map elevation, Hill 600 — and afterward as Dead Man’s Hill.[1][3]

Hill 689 was where 1/9 lived — the perimeter, the CP, the ops center. The battle of 16 April was fought on the other hill, a mile to its southwest.[1][3]

Sheet IV · The Battle

16 April 1968

That morning, Army air-cavalry scouts finishing Operation Pegasus spotted what the Marines most needed to know: all elements of the NVA 66th Regiment, 304th Division, had moved back into the hills near Route 9 and Lang Vei. The report never reached Marine commanders.[3] So when Company A stepped off its patrol at 0700, battalion believed the ridge a mile southwest held perhaps a squad. It held a fortified complex of a regiment that had been digging for weeks.

Use the phase buttons to replay the day on the map.

Daily journal · reconstructed · 16–17 April 1968
AM

Army air cavalry sights elements of the NVA 66th Regiment, 304th Division, back in the hills near Route 9 and Lang Vei. The report is never passed to Marine commanders.[3]

0700

Capt Henry D. Banks leads two reinforced platoons of Company A southwest off the Hill 689 perimeter.[2]

1000

Company A halts; two squads push onto a ridge in four-to-six-foot elephant grass and take small-arms and mortar fire from concealed bunkers. The first Marines fall.[2]

~1030

1stLt Michael P. Hayden’s 2d Platoon assaults; Hayden and then his platoon sergeant are killed in rapid succession. Alpha is pinned on the north end of the ridge — 10 dead, 20 wounded. Banks twice declines offered help, believing he faces a squad.[2]

~1200

Banks reverses and asks for relief.[2]

1320

LtCol Cahill commits Companies C and D. (His message doesn’t reach the regimental commander, Col Meyers, until 1543 — the radio-relay fog of that day.)[2]

~1400

Two platoons of Company C move out first — Capt Himmer leading, Cahill accompanying — and climb roughly 1,800 feet of the hill’s height toward the fight.[2][3]

~1430

Finding Alpha immobile on the north end, Cahill “ordered Himmer to attack from the south” — the veteran account has Charlie moving onto the eastern-southeastern ridge — while Delta presses from the northwest.[2][3]

PM

The relief attack bogs down in crossfire from bunkers, spider holes, and B-52 craters. Alpha’s dead and wounded are withdrawn. Somewhere on this southern approach, Captain Lawrence Himmer is killed leading his company. One of his Marines, PFC David Dee Brown Jr — four days in country — falls on the southern side of the hill.[3][13]

1745

Cahill orders every man off the hill with the wounded. The dead stay behind — “We will get them later.”[3]

night–0400

Entangled with the NVA in the dark, the companies work free and fall back northeast to Hill 689, completing the withdrawal in the early morning of 17 April.[1][7]

Sheet V · The Cost

Thirty-eight Marines, three corpsmen

Killed in action, 16–17 April38 USMC + 3 USN
Missing3
Wounded32
Recovery sweep by 2/3 Marines, four days later — the dead brought home+6 KIA · 86 WIA
July 1968: 1/1 Marines recover earlier dead at Hill 689 during the base evacuation+11 KIA

Official-history figures.[1][7] A veterans’ memorial page gives differing tallies for 16–19 April (9 KIA / 46 WIA / 36 MIA), likely reflecting confused initial field reporting; the official figures are treated as authoritative.[8]

Roughly one man in five who went up those slopes became a casualty in a single afternoon — among the worst days any Marine battalion endured in 1968. The battalion commander, LtCol John “Blackie” Cahill, was relieved of duty afterward; the roster shows his command passing to LtCol James W. Quinn on 13 May.[1][7] The official history states no reason. The record cuts both ways: he declined offered reinforcements and fed companies into a fortified position — yet the intelligence that would have changed everything was withheld above his level, and his caution about recovering the dead was echoed days later by regiment and division, who themselves suspended rescue attempts as too costly.[2][3] Cahill — Chosin Reservoir veteran, Silver Star, four Purple Hearts — retired a colonel and died in 2005.[9]

Sheet VI · Coming Home

Fort Rosecrans, Point Loma

Captain Himmer was brought home to San Diego and buried at Fort Rosecrans National Cemetery, Plot Q 1222, above the water at Point Loma — a few miles from Chula Vista.[14] His decorations include the Purple Heart, Combat Action Ribbon, Good Conduct Medal, National Defense Service Medal, Vietnam Service Medal, and Vietnam Campaign Medal.[5] His name is cut into Panel 50E, Line 14 of the Vietnam Veterans Memorial, among the men of the 16th of April.[4]

Six weeks after he fell, Jennifer was born. Fifty-two years after that, a Marine who had been on the hill found his page on the Wall of Faces and left eleven words about the Skipper. His company remembered him. His family still does.
